clinicalPearls: Autosomal recessive complicated hereditary spastic paraplegia caused by biallelic DSTYK variants; historically described as Lison syndrome.
The hallmark is spastic paraplegia combined with cutaneous pigmentary abnormalities - patchy hyperpigmented and hypopigmented (vitiligo-like) skin, i.e. dyschromatosis.
Premature greying of the hair and a characteristic facial appearance are additional clues that distinguish SPG23 from other HSP subtypes.
Neurological onset is usually in childhood with progressive lower-limb spasticity; some patients show mild cognitive or extrapyramidal features.
The skin changes often precede or accompany the neurological signs and should prompt DSTYK testing when they occur with spasticity.
Short stature and mildly dysmorphic facial features have been reported within affected kindreds.
Because the dermatological signs are the most readily recognisable marker, a joint neurology and dermatology assessment aids diagnosis.
reference.pathophysiology: SPG23 is caused by biallelic loss-of-function variants in DSTYK (dual serine/threonine and tyrosine protein kinase, also termed RIPK5), a dual-specificity kinase implicated in receptor tyrosine kinase signalling and in the regulation of programmed cell death. Loss of DSTYK function is thought to disturb signalling required for the survival and maintenance of specific neuronal populations, including corticospinal motor neurones, and of melanocyte and pigment-cell homeostasis, providing a unifying explanation for the combined neurological (spastic paraplegia) and pigmentary (dyschromatosis, premature hair greying) phenotype. Length-dependent degeneration of the corticospinal tracts produces the progressive lower-limb spasticity, while disrupted melanocyte function underlies the characteristic mixed hyper- and hypopigmentation of the skin and hair.
additionalDifferentials: SPG26 (B4GALNT1) - recessive complicated HSP with cognitive and extrapyramidal features (sibling subtype)
SPG11 (spatacsin) and SPG15 (spastizin) - recessive complicated HSPs with cognitive impairment
SPG7 (paraplegin) - recessive HSP with cerebellar, optic and neuropathic features
Isolated vitiligo or dyschromatosis symmetrica hereditaria with incidental neurological signs
Waardenburg syndrome and other pigmentary-neurological syndromes
additionalInvestigations: HSP gene panel or exome sequencing including DSTYK, with copy-number analysis
Dermatological review with clinical photography of pigmentary lesions and Wood's lamp examination
MRI of the brain and spine
Nerve conduction studies and EMG if a peripheral neuropathy is suspected
Neuropsychometric assessment to characterise any cognitive involvement
Skin biopsy only where the diagnosis of the pigmentary disorder is uncertain
redFlags: New or changing pigmented lesions with atypical features warranting exclusion of a cutaneous malignancy rather than assuming benign dyschromatosis
Rapid neurological deterioration or a sensory level suggesting an acquired myelopathy
Severe early cognitive regression prompting reconsideration of SPG11 or SPG15
reference.prognosis: Slowly progressive spasticity with a generally non-fatal course; the pigmentary and facial features are stable and are mainly of diagnostic rather than prognostic importance.
pitfalls: Treating the skin and neurological problems as unrelated and missing the unifying DSTYK diagnosis
Mistaking the vitiligo-like patches for isolated autoimmune vitiligo
Assuming normal cognition, when mild intellectual or extrapyramidal involvement can occur
references: Hereditary spastic paraplegia clinical review and classification
